records.bodyText:
The Western HVDC Link is a High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) undersea electrical link in the United Kingdom, between Hunterston in Western Scotland and Flintshire Bridge (Connah's Quay) in North Wales, routed to the west of the Isle of Man. It has a transmission capacity of 2,250 MW and became fully operational in 2019.
The project cost £1.2 billion to build.It was originally intended to enter service in 2015, and was given a deadline of 31 March 2017 by Ofgem, the industry regulator. In 2016, engineers working on the project discovered the almost intact wreck of the World War I German submarine UB-85. Completion was delayed a year due to cable manufacturing problems.
The link entered service on 7 December 2017 at a reduced capacity of 900 MW pending further work at Hunterston. Full use became available on 16 October 2018, but it did not give a full service until summer 2019, and was not formally handed over to the operator until 22 November 2019.
In November 2021, National Grid and ScottishPower agreed to pay a penalty of £158 million, after an Ofgem investigation determined these delays had increased consumer bills by limiting the amount of renewable power that could be sent from Scotland to the south of the UK. The investigation determined the delays were primarily caused by land acquisition problems, manufacturing problems, installation of cables and commissioning tests. £15 million of the penalty was paid into the regulator's redress scheme, which distributes money to charities and other organisations which help energy consumers; the rest was indirectly returned to consumers through changes to Ofgem's calculation of transmission costs in the national network.
The link augments the existing capacity provided by double-circuit AC transmission lines which join the Scottish and English transmission grids.
It consists of 422 km (262 miles) of cable, of which 385 km (239 miles) is under water. It is the first subsea link at 600 kV. Operating at this higher voltage increases transmission capacity and reduces transmission losses in the cable, reducing power loss from transmission and the two AC/DC conversions to under 3%. There are two cables, which in shallow water are laid in a paired bundle, and in deep water are laid about 30 m (98 ft) apart, generally buried about 1.5 m (5 ft) below the seabed. The cables are jointed in 120 km (75-mile) sections.
Line commutated converter technology is used at each HVDC converter to maximise the amount of electrical power that can be transferred, which is predominantly exported from renewable sources in Scotland. This type of HVDC conversion technology means that large filter halls are required at each converter station. Gas-insulated switchgear is used at the Hunterston converter station to save space.
Routing the connection through the Irish Sea, as opposed to a land-based route, reduced the impact of the link on the visual environment and prevented the rising cost of land affecting the cost of the project. For the given distance, it was necessary to use a DC transmission technology for a subsea route, as the capacitive current required for an AC connection would be too high. Due to the proximity of the converter stations to the coastline, a decision was taken to host electrical infrastructure within built structures in order to reduce the effects of the coastal air on the equipment.
Power can be transferred in either direction, but it is necessary for the link to be offline for a sufficient time prior to reversing the direction. Mass impregnated non-draining (MIND) cables are used in a bipolar arrangement, but no sea or earth return path is permitted for environmental reasons, meaning that both cables must be in service for the link to be operational. The cables are spaced apart to minimise thermal interference, but not so far as to materially impact any marine life which navigates using the magnetic field of the Earth.
The link has suffered a number of outages due to cable faults, which typically take several weeks to locate and fix:
• A fault in the southern land cable on 19 February 2019 resulted in an outage until 22 March.
•A further extended outage from 6 April 2019 was caused by a fault in the undersea cable.
• A third outage commenced on 10 January 2020,leading to Ofgem investigating.
• A fourth outage lasted from 15 February to 13 March 2021.— in Hunterston.

Western Link 2 HVDC Interconnector 
The next step has been taken in plans for the Western Link 2 electricity project linking Ayrshire with the west coast of Wales. SPEN are seeking a scoping opinion relating to the proposed HVDC subsea cable. The project is being jointly developed by National Grid and Scottish Power Energy Networks (SPEN).
The project involves a 13km underground cable linking a new converter station next to Kilmarnock South substation with a landfall point on the coast near Monkton.
There will be a 30km marine HVDC cable between Monkton and Grangestone, north of Girvan, and a new switching station at Grangestone.
Marine HVDC cables will then be laid heading south from Grangestone in Scottish waters.
The cable would carry electricity around 195 KM from Ayrshire to a landfall on the Gwynedd coastline. From there, underground cables would run to a proposed converter station near the existing Pentir substation. A new HVDC cable would connect the converter station to the substation.
The project is intended to support the transmission of renewable electricity between Scotland and Wales. It would be able to transmit about 2GW of electricity at 525kV.
A scoping opinion is now being sought, to see whether South Ayrshire Council requires an environmental impact assessment to be included in an overall planning application for the scheme.
The first Western Link, connecting Hunterston in Ayrshire with Connah’s Quay in North Wales, is already operating.
The scoping opinion application can be found on South Ayrshire Council's planning portal using reference 26/00734/EIASC
Key Project Specifications:
• Multi-terminal, 525 kV, 2 GW (HVDC) subsea and underground electrical link.
• Route Length is approx 340 km connecting
Scotland to Wales (with portions routing through or past waters around the Isle of Man).
• Scottish infrastructure components such as a 13 km underground cable linking a new converter station near Kilmarnock South substation to a landfall point, plus offshore cable runs from Monkton to Grangestone and a Grangestone switching station.
To strengthen the UK's transmission
network, integrate large-scale renewable energy (such as the 2GW MachairWind Offshore Windfarm), balance variable generation, and support the UK Net Zero transition.
Consultation phase highlighting preferred routes public consultation closed in late 2025, with ongoing scoping opinions and planning developments being sought through 2026 (such as scoping opinions for the Ayrshire cable route).— in Girvan, Ayrshire.

records.bodyText:
In an interesting turn of events, CEP have today quietly put back the date of their submission of an application for a Development Consent Order (DCO), which had been November of this year (ie now) to JULY 2027.
CWFL have now admitted their peat landslide hazard and risk assessment was wrong. As early as 10 July 2025 they told Natural England that Crow Hill had been stable since 1824, but they now admit the huge western bog burst was on 19 May 1989. Close examination of their own photographs shows ongoing instability. The national guidance, written by the CWFL consultant Dr Andy Mills, specifies avoidance as the primary mitigation. There are no realistic engineering solutions to bog burst except avoidance.
Haworth with Stanbury VC now hold a strong legal position, because they say the wind farm was designed and consulted on the false basis of Crow Hill being stable since 1824, and CWFL have now admitted to the council that the bog bursts are indeed ongoing.
The nine-month delay will not give CWFL time to redesign and reconsult the proposal away from Crow Hill. Instead it allows Algihaz to pause spending on a shoal of expensive minor matters while they work out what they can do. Algihaz have been kept fully informed by Stronger Together, and it is likely that they have asked for an independent report. The stability errors on Crow Hill are so significant, and the common law legal position of Haworth with Stanbury VC so strong, that the proposal as it stands can be snuffed out in a morning in court, even if Miatta Fahnbulleh (who is the sole decider) gives consent.
You can read Walshaw Turbine Research Group's formal report on Crow Hill here: https://stopcalderdaleenergypark.com/calderdale-wind.../
https://www.calderdaleenergypark.co.uk/proposed.../

records.title: Our Power
records.bodyText:
Shetland community energy groups urge Scottish Government to switch to multi-year funding!
Development companies and community energy officers across Shetland are calling on Public Finance Minister (and local MSP) Hannah Mary Goodlad to overhaul the Scottish Government’s Community and Renewable Energy Scheme (CARES).
Under the current annual system, grants awarded in the autumn must be spent by mid-March. Local groups say this rigid timeline creates unnecessary barriers:
-Pushes construction directly into harsh winter months
-Forces large-scale renewable projects into fragmented phases
-Increases overheads through repeated procurement cycles
With community bodies from Bressay, Sandwick, North Yell, Northmavine, Scalloway, and beyond backing the joint letter, the message ahead of the upcoming Scottish budget is clear: long-term projects need long-term funding certainty.

Ofgem Names Preferred Bidder for Dogger Bank B Offshore Transmission Assets
Dogger Bank Wind Farm
A consortium of Diamond Transmission UK (DTUK) and Japan’s Chubu Electric Power has been selected as the preferred bidder to acquire and operate the offshore transmission assets connecting the 1.2 GW Dogger Bank B wind farm to the national grid.
The transmission system, valued at approximately £1B (around €1.2B ) by the consortium, comprises subsea and onshore cables, an offshore converter station and an onshore converter station.
The consortium will operate the transmission business for 25 years after acquiring the assets and receiving an Offshore Transmission Owner (OFTO) licence from the UK energy regulator.
The preferred bidder appointment is part of Ofgem’s Tender Round 11 process.
Ofgem launched the tender round in February 2024 and shortlisted four bidder groups in July that year. Ofgem appointed the consortium of DTUK and Chubu as the preferred bidder on 5 November 2026.
Dogger Bank B, located approximately 130 KM off the UK’s east coast, is the second phase of the world’s largest offshore wind farm under construction, the 3.6 GW Dogger Bank Wind Farm, owned by the consortium of SSE Renewables, Equinor, and Vårgrønn.
The second phase (Doggar Bank 3) is currently under construction, with wind turbine installation underway, the WTG components being loaded at port of Nigg in the highlands.
— at North Sea.

I am sharing this Shona Paterson's comment  on an earlier post because it sums up so many things about what is happening in Scotland. She nails the sentiment felt throughout rural Scotland.
______________________________________________________
'We have been doing our best to get the message across for years. We as residents of the Highlands who have been fighting against the destruction of our local landscapes and wildlife habitats, the killing of our birds, the pollution of our rivers, the cutting down of our trees, the massive amount of carbon and greenhouse gases being released into our atmosphere to be replaced by millions of tonnes of reinforced concrete, all to make foreign companies and their already rich shareholders even richer, while the UK taxpayers and bill payers are robbed even more: say enough is enough!!
The people of the threatened local communities are exhausted by this fight. Community Councils are overwhelmed by this fight and when Highland Council has been repeatedly saying that this is wrong and oppose it and now other councils are also saying a big NO. Why are the Scottish government able to continue to overrule us all and all local democracy and all the scientific evidence and basic common sense?? Why?? How can we stand up for the rural communities, our wonderful scenic landscapes, our fantastic wildlife, ecology and biodiversity and the local and Scottish economy and ordinary UK residents being forced to pay for our governments total madness. This is meant to be a democracy not an dictatorship!'
